context: The word is Dante's invention. This canto and the twelve after it, to Inferno 30, are spent crossing its ten ditches one by one.

note: The sheer cliff that Dante and Virgil have just flown down. It walls Malebolge off from the seventh circle above.
The pit at the center of Hell. Giants stand around its rim, and at its bottom lies the ninth and last circle, the frozen lake of the traitors (Inferno 31–34).
Ten ring-shaped ditches, one inside the other, each for a different kind of fraud. The ground slopes inward, so each ditch lies a little lower than the one before.

quote: a castle surrounded by multiple moats
note: Malebolge is laid out like a fortress seen from above: ring after ring of moats, crossed by bridges. But this fortress has nothing at its center except a hole.

Natural bridges of rock that run like the spokes of a wheel from the outer cliff to the central well, arching over each ditch. Dante and Virgil walk along one of them and look down from the top of each arch.

context: The monster has just flown the two poets down the cliff from the seventh circle and set them at its foot (Inferno 17).

note: The poets nearly always turn left as they go down through Hell. Left was the side of evil, and on the mountain of Purgatory they will turn right.
The punishment fits the sin. Panders and seducers drove others on to serve someone's lust, and now they are driven on themselves, without rest.
Two files move in opposite directions. The nearer file, facing the poets, is the panders, who procured women for other men. The farther file is the seducers, who deceived women for themselves.

1300, the year of Dante's journey. Pope Boniface VIII proclaimed it the first Jubilee, or Holy Year, promising pardon of sins to pilgrims who visited the great churches of Rome. The crowds were enormous. The detail is so exact that Dante may have seen it himself.
The Ponte Sant'Angelo, then the main way across the Tiber to St. Peter's. A barrier down the middle kept pilgrims going and pilgrims returning apart: an early case of two-way traffic.
Castel Sant'Angelo, the tomb of the emperor Hadrian turned into a papal fortress. It stands at the end of the bridge on the St. Peter's side.
Usually taken to be Monte Giordano, a small rise in the city on the other side of the river.
The first devils of the traditional kind in the poem, with horns and whips. Malebolge is full of them.

Venedico Caccianemico, a leader of the Guelph party in Bologna who governed several cities as chief magistrate. Dante seems to have thought him dead by 1300. The records show that he lived a few years longer.
Dante's Italian says "such pungent sauces". Early commentators heard a local joke in it: the Salse was a ravine outside Bologna where the bodies of executed criminals were thrown.
Ghisolabella, Venedico's own sister. He is said to have handed her over to the Marquis for money or for political favor.
A marquis of the Este family, lords of Ferrara: usually taken to be Obizzo II, whom Dante has already shown among the tyrants in the river of blood (Inferno 12). Some say his son Azzo VIII.

quote: however that shameful story gets told
note: The scandal evidently went around in more than one version. Venedico settles it by confessing.

context: Venedico says there are more Bolognese pimps in this ditch than there are people now living in Bologna.

note: The old Bolognese dialect word for "yes". To say sipa is to be from Bologna.
The two rivers that pass on either side of Bologna, to the west and the east.

quote: There are no women here to sell
note: The Italian is harsher and has a double sense: "femmine da conio" can mean women to be turned into coin, or women to be tricked.
The second file, the seducers. They were moving the same way as the poets, so Dante saw only their backs. From the bridge he can look them in the face.

quote: What a royal bearing he still maintains!
note: The one soul in this ditch given any dignity. He doesn't weep or run, and Virgil speaks of him almost with admiration. The fraud was real all the same.

context: He is here as a seducer, for the two women he won with fine words and then abandoned: Hypsipyle and Medea.

note: A kingdom at the eastern end of the Black Sea, in what is now Georgia. Its king kept the Golden Fleece, the fleece of a magical ram, guarded by a dragon.
An island in the northern Aegean. In the myth, Venus cursed the women of Lemnos, their husbands turned away from them, and the women agreed to kill every man on the island in a single night.

context: She had "deceived all the others" by pretending to kill her father, the king, while secretly helping him escape. The deceiver was then deceived by Jason.
The betrayal is Jason's betrayal of her. She helped him win the Fleece and fled with him, and he later left her for another bride.

note: The ditch of the flatterers. They sink in excrement, an image of what their words were worth. Dante gives the place a short, deliberately coarse scene and moves on.
A priest was known by his tonsure, the shaved crown of his head. This head is too filthy for Dante to tell whether it is shaved or not.
A man of a noble family of Lucca, the Interminelli. Documents show him alive in 1295. Almost nothing else is known of him except what Dante says here.

Not a real woman but a character in The Eunuch, a comedy by the Roman playwright Terence. Dante probably knew the scene from Cicero, who quotes it as an example of flattery. In the play the gushing answer is given by a go-between, not by Thaïs herself.
Her lover had sent her a slave girl as a present and asked whether she was grateful. Flattery is a small thing beside the sins above and below it, but Dante treats it as fraud: words sold for gain.
